title: Plant omega-3 vs. fish omega-3: ALA, EPA, and DHA explained

seo.title: Plant omega-3 vs. fish omega-3: ALA, EPA, DHA
seo.meta_description: Chia, flax, and walnuts mainly provide ALA; fatty fish provides EPA and DHA directly. The amounts are not nutritionally interchangeable gram for gram.
seo.search_intent: Understand the difference between plant omega-3 and fish omega-3, including ALA, EPA, DHA, conversion, and practical food sources.

excerpt: Chia, flax, and walnuts can deliver several grams of ALA, while salmon and sardines supply EPA and DHA directly. All are omega-3 fats, but a gram of ALA is not the same as a gram of EPA or DHA because human conversion is limited.
content_html:
The phrase contains omega-3 hides an important distinction. Most plant foods provide alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), while fatty fish provides the long-chain omega-3 fats EPA and DHA directly.

ALA, EPA, and DHA are related, not interchangeable

ALA is an essential fatty acid, meaning the body cannot make enough of it and it has to come from food. Flax, chia, walnuts, soybean oil, and canola oil are important sources. EPA and DHA are concentrated in fish and seafood and can also come from microalgae-based products.

The body can convert ALA to EPA and then DHA, but NIH describes that conversion as very limited, with reported conversion rates below 15% and DHA formation especially small. That is why 5 grams of ALA should not be read as 5 grams of EPA+DHA.

What common servings actually provide

FoodServingMain omega-3Approx. amount
Chia seeds1 oz (28 g)ALA~5.06 g
English walnuts1 oz (28 g)ALA~2.57 g
Whole flaxseed1 tbspALA~2.35 g
Farmed Atlantic salmon, cooked3 oz (85 g)EPA+DHA~1.83 g
Canned sardines, drained3 oz (85 g)EPA+DHA~1.19 g

Chia has more total omega-3 by weight in that serving than salmon, but almost all of it is ALA. Salmon delivers EPA and DHA already in long-chain form.

Does that make plant omega-3 inferior?

No. ALA is essential and useful in its own right. The mistake is treating ALA and EPA+DHA as if they were metabolically identical. A well-designed diet can include both rather than choosing a winner.

For people who do not eat fish, nuts and seeds remain valuable sources of ALA. If the goal is to obtain DHA or EPA directly without fish, algal oil is the most direct non-fish option.

Fish varies enormously too

“Fish” is not a useful single number for long-chain omega-3. NIH lists about 1.83 g EPA+DHA in 3 oz of cooked farmed Atlantic salmon but only about 0.14 g in 3 oz of cooked Pacific cod. That is a difference of roughly 1.7 g in the same serving weight.

Fatty species such as salmon, sardines, mackerel, and herring therefore play a different omega-3 role from very lean white fish.

How much ALA do adults need?

The U.S. Adequate Intake for ALA is 1.6 g/day for adult men and 1.1 g/day for adult women, with separate values during pregnancy and lactation. There is no FDA Daily Value specifically for EPA and DHA, which is one reason food guidance often uses seafood servings rather than one universal EPA+DHA percentage.

The useful comparison

If you want to know whether a food provides ALA, look at ALA. If you want EPA and DHA, look directly at EPA and DHA. Adding all three together under one “omega-3” number can obscure what the food actually contributes.

faq.question: Is omega-3 from chia the same as omega-3 from salmon?
faq.answer: No. Chia mainly provides ALA; salmon supplies EPA and DHA directly. Human conversion of ALA to the long-chain forms is limited.

faq.question: Are walnuts high in omega-3?
faq.answer: Yes, as ALA. One ounce provides about 2.57 g ALA, but that should not be interpreted as 2.57 g EPA+DHA.

faq.question: Can you get DHA without eating fish?
faq.answer: Yes. Microalgae-derived oils can provide DHA and, depending on the product, EPA without fish.
